```{r setup}
library(cyclingpower)
library(dplyr)
```

Two power meters on the same bike rarely agree exactly, and the interesting
question is not whether they differ but by how much, and whether the gap is
steady or opens up as you push harder. This vignette walks through that
comparison, then through the harder case where a third meter has to be brought
onto the same scale without ever having been ridden alongside the first.

We work from the ride bundled with the package and manufacture a second and
third meter from it with distortions we choose, so there is a known answer to
check the results against. Everything here assumes the files already exist;
`vignette("recording_rides")` covers how to record them, and several of the
decisions there — recording rate, auto-pause, and what to actually ride —
determine whether the steps below can work at all.

```{r data}
ride <- read_file(system.file("extdata", "power1.fit", package = "cyclingpower"))
ride
```

Every reader returns this same shape whatever the file format, so a GPX
exported from Strava and a FIT pulled off a head unit arrive with the same
column names and types. `time` and `power` are always present; the other
channels appear when the file carries them.

## Getting files into the comparison

The unit of analysis is a run, meaning one session ridden once, recorded by two
or more sources. `read_rides()` takes that structure as an explicit table of
paths, runs and sources rather than inferring it, and `ride_spec_from_names()`
builds one from a `run1_kickr.fit` naming convention when your files already
follow it. A filename that does not split cleanly is an error rather than a
silently missing label.

Here we fabricate the files instead. Meter B reads three per cent high, and its
head unit's clock runs seven seconds fast.

```{r build}
b <- ride
b$power <- ride$power * 1.03
b$time <- ride$time + 7

rides <- bind_rows(
  mutate(ride, run = "run1", source = "A", .before = 1),
  mutate(b, run = "run1", source = "B", .before = 1)
)
```

## Putting the sources on one clock

That seven-second offset matters more than it looks. Differencing the two
series on their nominal timestamps compares power from one moment against power
from another, which inflates the spread and shifts the average difference, and
nothing about the result announces that it has happened. `align_rides()`
resamples each source onto a one-second grid and recovers the offset by
cross-correlating the power traces.

```{r align}
aligned <- align_rides(rides)
alignment_report(aligned)
```

The report is worth reading rather than skipping. `offset` is the correction
applied, `correlation` how well the traces matched at that offset, and `status`
whether the offset was established at all. Where both channels came off a
single head unit the offset is simply zero and the same code path serves. Where
a ride was too steady to lock onto — a long block at constant power has no
features to align against — the status comes back `unresolved`, the recorded
timestamps stand, and a warning says so.

## How far apart do they read?

```{r agreement}
power_agreement(aligned)
```

`bias_w` is the average difference in watts and `gain_pc` the same thing
multiplicatively, which is usually the more natural way to think about a power
meter, since meters tend to be a few per cent out rather than a fixed number of
watts out. We built B to read three per cent high, so A relative to B comes back
at `1/1.03 - 1`, or about −2.9 per cent. The limits of agreement bound the range
within which most individual seconds fall.

The intervals come from a moving-block bootstrap rather than from treating each
second as an independent observation. Per-second power is heavily
autocorrelated — what you are riding now is nearly what you were riding a second
ago — so an hour's recording carries far less independent information than its
3,600 rows suggest, and an interval built on the independence assumption would
be roughly an order of magnitude too narrow.

```{r bland-altman}
plot_agreement(aligned)
```

## Does the gap change with effort?

A single average difference hides the pattern that usually matters, which is a
meter agreeing at endurance pace and drifting at threshold.
`agreement_by_level()` bins the seconds by the mean of the two readings and
reports the difference within each band.

Binning on the mean rather than on one nominated meter is deliberate. If you bin
by meter A and then plot A minus B against those bins, A's own measurement noise
pushes the points into a slope, and you see a trend that is an artefact of the
plotting rather than a property of the meters.

```{r by-level}
by_level <- agreement_by_level(aligned, width = 25)
plot_by_level(by_level)
```

`seconds` travels with every row because time is not spread evenly across the
power range. The ends are usually thin, and an estimate resting on twenty
seconds deserves less weight than one resting on six hundred.

## Bringing in a third meter

Now the awkward case. Suppose run one carried meters A and B, and run two
carried B and C. A and C have never been on the bike together, so there is no
second at which both were measuring. B is the bridge: each run gives a gain
relative to B, and the difference between those two gains is A against C.

```{r three-way}
first <- ride[1:1800, ]
second <- ride[1801:3601, ]

scale_power <- function(x, gain) {
  x$power <- x$power * gain
  x
}

three_way <- bind_rows(
  mutate(scale_power(first, 1.00), run = "run1", source = "A", .before = 1),
  mutate(scale_power(first, 1.03), run = "run1", source = "B", .before = 1),
  mutate(scale_power(second, 1.03), run = "run2", source = "B", .before = 1),
  mutate(scale_power(second, 0.97), run = "run2", source = "C", .before = 1)
)

chained <- three_way |>
  align_rides() |>
  chain_sources()

chained
```

A against C comes back at about 3.1 per cent, which is `1.00 / 0.97 - 1`, and
the `basis` column marks it as chained rather than directly observed. That
distinction is the point: the two direct comparisons rest on seconds where both
meters measured the same effort, while the chained one rests on an assumption
as well.

```{r chain-plot}
plot_chain(chained)
```

The assumption is that B read the same on both days, and nothing in the ride
files can test it. A meter that drifted between the two sessions moves the
A-to-C figure by exactly the amount it drifted, and the data offer no way to
tell that apart from a genuine difference between A and C. `chain_report()`
states this and reports what can be checked, which is whether the two runs
covered comparable power — gains estimated over different parts of the range
are not really comparable at all.

```{r chain-report}
report <- chain_report(chained)
report$overlap
report$coverage
```

## Doing all of it at once

`compare_report()` runs this whole sequence from a set of files and writes it
out as a single HTML document, which is usually what you want once the
exploration is done.

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
list.files("rides", full.names = TRUE) |>
  ride_spec_from_names() |>
  compare_report("power-comparison.html")
```
